## VERDICT

**1. Rung 1 FAILS, and not narrowly.  No rule x arm clears $2,000/day realised in any era — the best cell in the whole grid is $242/day and the best 2024-25 cell is $70/day.**  Across 5 eras x 5 arms x 6 implementable rules x 2 basket sizes (300 cells) realised P&L runs -$187 to +$242/day, i.e. -12% to +16% of the picked band.  The best cell per era, top-5: `blind_e3` $173 (v2, patience), `e4` $63 (E/T/I, patience), `e5` $15 (E/T/I, close), `e6` $63 (v2 no-M, patience), `e7` $41 (v2, close).  Top-3 is the same picture with a smaller denominator: $242 / $113 / $67 / $70 / $59.  No mirror variant beats hold-to-close by a margin that survives moving one era, and the ranking of the six rules changes era to era — which is itself the finding that none of them is a rule.

**2. WHY, exactly: the confirmation is paid TWICE, and it costs the whole leg.**  Measured over every picked candidate in every era: the pivot-to-pivot leg is worth **$285-$427** gross on the $100k object ($366-$427 in the 2024-25 eras).  The confirmed-extreme ENTRY has already spent **$156-$228** of that leg before we are filled (price must retrace the threshold off the extreme to confirm it, then the roster waits its 60-120s).  The mirror EXIT spends another **$135-$198** confirming that the far turn happened.  What is left is **-$6 to +$14 gross**, then the 576c round trip takes it.  A confirmation-in / confirmation-out trade on the same threshold nets zero BY CONSTRUCTION.  That is why the multiplier grid does not rescue it: x1.5 makes the exit giveback bigger ($200 -> larger) without making the leg longer, x0.75 exits before the leg develops (mean hold 8-11 min against x1.0's 13-21 min), and both land within $100/day of x1.0 in every era.

**3. The mirror DOES work as a dud-cutter — and cuts winners at exactly the same rate.**  Per trade, hold-to-close pays $280-$599 on candidates that were winners and -$223 to -$276 on duds; `mirror@1.00` pays $108-$189 on winners and -$43 to -$81 on duds.  It is a clean, symmetric compression of both tails.  With a 28-34% winner share the two cancel to zero.  Nothing in this rung distinguishes the two classes, which is the same conclusion the EXIT CENSUS reached from the other side: exits need STATE, not a price-symmetric rule.

**4. A second, bigger structural finding: the picked band is NOT reachable with one position, by any exit rule whatsoever.**  One-position occupancy alone removes 45-50% of the top-5 picked value before any exit rule is applied — only **2.0-2.4 of the 5 daily picks are enterable** one at a time (1.6-1.9 of 3).  The perfect-exit ceiling — the oracle certificate of the picks actually ENTERED — is **$978 / $1,052 / $907 / $1,008 / $1,144 per day** at top-5 and $805 / $814 / $712 / $837 / $892 at top-3.  So D-045's target as literally stated ("capture near 100% of the $2,000-2,225 picked band") is arithmetically impossible for a one-contract, one-position system: the ceiling is about **$1,000/day**.  The honest measure is capture of the ENTERED certificate, and on that measure every implementable rule scores -29% to +23% while the oracle scores 101-105% (the small overshoot is the grid-mid fill envelope, quantified in the calibration section).  Getting to $2,000/day needs one of: a second concurrent position, entries whose certificates are individually larger, or both — it cannot come from the exit alone.

**5. The ratchet never armed.**  0.5 x the training window's median winner MFE is $427-$432 (training medians $854-$863), and the mirror exit fires at a mean hold of 18-20 minutes, long before a typical trade reaches that level.  `mirror@1.00+ratchet` is byte-identical to `mirror@1.00` in four of five eras and differs by under $2/day in `e7`.  Reported as run; it is not a rule that was tried and failed, it is a rule that never fired.

**6. What this hands to rung 2.**  (a) The exit must be CLASS-CONDITIONAL — the oracle's winner trades average $959-$1,092 and even its dud trades average +$133-$197, so the entire prize sits in telling the two apart at the exit second, not in any threshold.  (b) The entry-side giveback is now measured at $156-$228 — half the leg — and is worth exactly as much as any exit improvement; a rung that recovers part of it (partial fill nearer the extreme, or an entry threshold whose legs are proportionally longer) buys as much as a perfect exit does.  (c) The $300 wall binds on 65-73% of hold-to-close trades, which is why the fixed-close baseline is near zero rather than positive; the wall and the exit rule are one design problem, not two.

**Controls.**  The grid-mid replay is calibrated against the truth leaf on the identical candidates: mean `close` +$9/trade against `menu_net_cent[close]` (correlation 0.968) and mean `oracle` +$15/trade against `certificate_net_cent`, i.e. the grid-mid envelope is about one half-spread per side more generous than the conservative ask/bid kernel and does not change any verdict above.  Costs are charged on every trade of every rule.  The wall is retained with gap-through.  Every rule in the grid was fixed by the brief before any number was computed and all of them are reported.  Sealed zone untouched (highest session replayed: 917).  D-022 overlay: era RTY factors run 0.879-1.073, so the RTY-mini equivalents of every figure above are within 12% of the dollars shown and change nothing.
